name: While You're Here
tagline: A shop prices its surprises from its own history before the job starts, so saying yes and getting paid are the same tap.
old_product: The carbon-copy job ticket, the estimate pad and the unwritten 'while you're here, can you also…' extra
fresh_spin: At quote time the homeowner signs a capped menu of likely surprises with honest odds from the shop's own invoices, and mid-job her tap on that list is the change order.
boring_but: Boring on the surface, it's a change-order form. But the shop prices its surprises from its own history before the job starts, so saying yes and getting paid are the same tap.
borrows_from: Counter (fresh spin 04): ranges proposed from the business's own invoices, approved by the owner
#35 Lookahead: a forecast the contractor commits to in advance and is held to
Posted (fresh spin 02): every approval sealed with a timestamp into one evidence pack
summary: While You're Here is a $49-a-month Jobber app plus a $99 menu build for 2-6-person remodelers, handymen and electricians. It pulls quote and invoice line items through Jobber's GraphQL API, diffs them, and proposes a surprise menu: hidden conditions with locked odds ('31 of 80 jobs') and ranges, plus pre-priced add-ons. The owner prunes and approves. The homeowner signs the menu with the quote under a plain top line ('Your price $8,400. At most $10,100, only if we find…'), with the worst case capped at 25% of base. The menu stays live on her phone as 'Your job list': she taps add-ons herself, and hidden-condition lines bill only with a photo and her tap after ESIGN e-consent. Each tap is written back to Jobber as a signed change order and sealed into an evidence pack; off-menu extras get a plain approval link.
first_buyer: The owner of a 2-6-person remodeling, handyman or electrical shop already paying for Jobber, the week after a homeowner refused to pay for an unwritten extra.
why_now: Jobber still has no change-order module; its own community thread documents the second-quote workaround, and add-ons such as JobAmend have appeared to fill it. Jobber's GraphQL API and app marketplace (100+ integrations) make a plug-in feasible. Jobber's AI Receptionist books jobs from a phone description before anyone sees the wall, which pushes more scope discovery mid-job. Business apps have the best first annual renewal (40%). There is no dated legal trigger: written change-order statutes (California B&P 7159.6, Pennsylvania HICPA, New Jersey, Massachusetts 142A) are long-standing.
competitors: JobAmend: Jobber change-order approval app, free until the first approved change order, then $29/month flat (vendor post)
Jobber: quotes with required client signatures; change orders handled by revising or adding quotes
ScopeProof: standalone change-order app (no information found)
Buildertrend (absorbed CoConstruct), Knowify, Contractor Foreman, Houzz Pro, Projul: native signed change orders for remodelers, roughly $50-500/month (unverified)
Housecall Pro and ServiceTitan: change orders through revised estimates (pricing unverified)
Joist: low-cost estimate and invoice app (pricing unverified)
price_and_margin: $49/month plus a $99 menu build. Cost to serve about $1/month (SMS, storage, API calls), so about 98% gross margin. Assumed CAC about $250 and 3.5% monthly churn give about $1,400 lifetime revenue per shop, about 5.6x CAC (assumptions, unverified).
channel: First 100: the 10 concierge-test shops, the Jobber community change-order thread, Jobber user Facebook groups and NARI chapters, founder-led. First 1,000: the Jobber App Marketplace listing after App Review, homeowners' 'Your job list' pages exposing other shops' customers, and referrals; Housecall Pro and QuickBooks later.
demand_test: Four weeks with 10 Jobber shops from the forum and Facebook groups: $99 for a hand-built menu from their invoice export, alternating menu and plain quotes. Measure add-on dollars per job, extras collected versus written off, close rate (directional on about 200 quotes), and how many shops' invoices yield five or more usable menu lines. Go if 6 of 10 pay and menu jobs bring $150+ more, or close rate rises 5+ points.
mvp_90_days: Weeks 1-4: concierge test from invoice exports. Weeks 3-9: Jobber OAuth app, GraphQL pull of quote and invoice line items, diff with catalog matching plus fuzzy matching for free-text lines, owner approval, capped menu builder with locked odds, 'Your job list' homeowner page with ESIGN e-consent, tap-to-add, photo-required hidden conditions, timestamp seal, write-back to the Jobber job. Weeks 10-13: Jobber App Review and listing, 25 paying shops.
kill_metric: Fewer than 6 of 10 test shops paying; by month 6, under 75 paying shops, churn over 5% a month, or under 40% of menu jobs with at least one homeowner tap.
risks: Jobber builds native change orders (likely within two years), making approval free
Messy data: free-text and lump-sum invoices hide extras, so many shops yield few usable menu lines
Lowball-then-upcharge abuse would be an FTC Act and state UDAP problem; mitigated by full-scope base price, locked odds with counts, a 25% cap, photo proof and declinable lines
State change-order statutes: a tap must carry the required fields, contractor signature and prior ESIGN consumer consent; counsel needed in California and Pennsylvania before launch
No measured data on how often extras go unpaid, and no dated trigger
Techs skip the app mid-job rather than look petty; the homeowner-tap design must make it easier than saying yes
Jobber marketplace terms and revenue share are not public
three_year: Housecall Pro and QuickBooks histories added; pooled, anonymised regional odds ('rot in 38% of pre-1970 bathrooms in this county') so new shops can quote honestly; if Jobber goes native, approval goes free and the odds engine and regional data become the product or an acquisition. Target 3-5k shops, about $2-3M ARR.
best_line: 'At most $10,100' is a promise a lowballer can't print.
